claim: Eucalyptus melliodora is a foundation species of a critically endangered community in Australia that is a target for restoration.
source: Eucalyptus melliodora is a foundation species of a critically endangered community in Australia that is a target for restoration.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction regarding the endangered status of the White Box–Yellow Box–Blakely's Red Gum Grassy Woodland community.

claim: The study examined genomic and phenotypic variation in E. melliodora across 275 individuals from 36 sites.
source: Here we survey genomic variation in 275 individuals from 36 sites across the present range of E. melliodora.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction and supported by the methods and results sections describing the sampling and analysis.

claim: High levels of gene flow extend for 500 km in E. melliodora.
source: We examined isolation by distance and isolation by environment, determining high levels of gene flow extending for 500 km and correlations with climate and soil variables.
evidence: Based on the GDM model showing no genomic differentiation until close to 500 km geographic distance.

claim: Genomic variation in E. melliodora correlates with climate and soil variables.
source: We examined isolation by distance and isolation by environment, determining high levels of gene flow extending for 500 km and correlations with climate and soil variables.
evidence: Supported by GDM analysis identifying significant environmental predictors including nitrogen, temperature, precipitation, and isothermality.

claim: Growth experiments revealed extensive phenotypic variation both within and among sampling sites.
source: Growth experiments revealed extensive phenotypic variation both within and among sampling sites, but no site-specific differentiation in phenotypic plasticity.
evidence: Demonstrated by statistical analyses showing significant effects of sampling site and maternal line on growth traits.

claim: No site-specific differentiation in phenotypic plasticity was found in E. melliodora.
source: Growth experiments revealed extensive phenotypic variation both within and among sampling sites, but no site-specific differentiation in phenotypic plasticity.
evidence: Supported by linear mixed-effect models showing no significant interaction between sampling site/maternal line and experimental condition.

claim: Seed can be sourced broadly across the landscape for E. melliodora restoration.
source: Model predictions suggest that seed can be sourced broadly across the landscape, providing ample diversity for adaptation to environmental change.
evidence: Based on the finding of low genetic differentiation over large spatial scales and high gene flow extending 500 km.

claim: Species face rapid environmental change often in combination with habitat loss and fragmentation.
source: Species around the globe face rapidly changing environments, often in combination with habitat loss and fragmentation.
evidence: General statement supported by citation to Lindenmayer et al., 2010.

claim: Rapid environmental change and habitat loss are expected to have a negative impact on biodiversity.
source: These factors are expected to have a negative impact on biodiversity (Lindenmayer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lindenmayer et al., 2010.

claim: Three processes enable species to survive altered conditions: migration, adaptation, and phenotypic plasticity.
source: Three processes enable species to survive altered conditions: migration, adaptation, and phenotypic plasticity (Aitken and Whitlock, 2013; Aitken et al., 2008; Hoffmann et al., 2015; Nicotra et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Seed sourcing during landscape restoration provides an opportunity to apply scientific knowledge to improve conservation outcomes.
source: Seed sourcing during landscape restoration provides an ideal opportunity to apply scientific knowledge to enable these key processes and improve conservation outcomes (Broadhurst et al., 2008; Prober et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Broadhurst et al., 2008 and Prober et al., 2015.

claim: Historically, restoration has often focused on geographically restricted local sources of seed.
source: Historically, restoration has often focused on geographically restricted local sources of seed under the premise that this would improve restoration outcomes by reducing the risk of maladaptation to local conditions and by preventing outbreeding depression (Broadhurst et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broadhurst et al., 2008.

claim: Narrow local seed sourcing reduces the pool of available genetic material in fragmented systems.
source: In a fragmented system, narrow local seed sourcing reduces the number of potential source populations, thereby reducing the pool of available genetic material.
evidence: Logical inference from the description of fragmented systems and seed sourcing practices.

claim: Reduced gene pool may result in inbreeding depression in future generations, especially if combined with small population size.
source: This reduced gene pool may result in inbreeding depression in future generations, especially if combined with small population size (Broadhurst et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broadhurst et al., 2008.

claim: Obtaining seed from a wider geographical area can increase genomic and phenotypic diversity.
source: Obtaining seed from a wider geographical area can increase genomic and phenotypic diversity, thereby increasing the ability of the species to survive in situ (Broadhurst et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broadhurst et al., 2008.

claim: Climate adjusted provenancing provides a seed sourcing strategy that focuses on both genetic diversity and adaptability under predicted future conditions.
source: In recent years, climate adjusted provenancing has been proposed, providing a seed sourcing strategy that focuses on both genetic diversity and adaptability under predicted future conditions (Byrne et al., 2013; Prober et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Byrne et al., 2013 and Prober et al., 2015.

claim: Eucalyptus melliodora is commonly called yellow box.
source: Eucalyptus melliodora (A.Cunn. ex Schauer), commonly called yellow box, is an iconic Australian tree that is the subject of extensive restoration efforts across its distribution.
evidence: Direct statement of common name.

claim: The White Box–Yellow Box–Blakely's Red Gum Grassy Woodland and Derived Native Grassland is a critically endangered ecological community.
source: It is a foundation species of a critically endangered ecological community: the White Box–Yellow Box–Blakely's Red Gum Grassy Woodland and Derived Native Grassland (Department of Environment and Climate Change and Water, 2011; Department of the Environment and Heritage, 2006; Threatened Species Scientific Committee, 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple government citations.

claim: Less than 5% of the original distribution of the White Box–Yellow Box–Blakely's Red Gum Grassy Woodland community remains.
source: This woodland community exists in a fragmented landscape, with less than 5% of its original distribution remaining, mostly in small remnant patches (Department of Environment and Climate Change and Water, 2011; Department of the Environment and Heritage, 2006; Threatened Species Scientific Committee, 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple government citations.

claim: Species distribution modelling predicts that most eucalypts will need to shift their distributions considerably in response to climate change.
source: Climate change is an important consideration in seed sourcing decisions because species distribution modelling predicts that most eucalypts will need to shift their distributions considerably in response (González-Orozco et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Orozco et al., 2016.

claim: Ecological niche modelling predicts that by 2090 the E. melliodora distribution will shift toward the southeast and suitable areas will decrease by 77%.
source: In particular, ecological niche modelling for E. melliodora predicts that by 2090 the species distribution will shift toward the southeast and suitable areas will decrease by 77% as a result of environmental changes (Broadhurst et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broadhurst et al., 2018.

claim: The study sequenced Genotyping by Sequencing (GBS) libraries for each sample using Illumina sequencing.
source: For each sample we Illumina sequenced a Genotyping by Sequencing (GBS) library (Elshire et al., 2011) and used a reference alignment approach to call genotypes.
evidence: Direct description of methods used.

claim: 69 samples were removed due to greater than 60% missing data.
source: We conducted a preliminary analysis based on 123,227 SNPs and removed 69 samples due to greater than 60% missing data.
evidence: Direct statement of data filtering procedure.

claim: 19 samples were identified as strong genomic outliers, likely misidentified samples or recent hybrids.
source: A preliminary principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) identified 19 samples that were strong genomic outliers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), likely misidentified samples or recent hybrids.
evidence: Based on PCoA analysis and supported by morphological differences and previous microsatellite work.

claim: The final dataset included 275 samples from 36 sites genotyped at 9,378 physically distinct SNPs.
source: The final data set included 275 samples from 36 sites (Figure 1A), genotyped at 9,378 physically distinct SNPs (>300 bp apart).
evidence: Direct statement of final dataset composition.

claim: Technical replicates cluster closely together in the genomic distance dendrogram.
source: Visual examination of a cluster dendrogram of genomic distance between samples showed that technical replicates cluster closely together (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on visual examination of dendrogram.

claim: The PCoA of genomic distance among samples showed continuous variation with little suggestion of discrete population structure.
source: The PCoA of genomic distance among samples showed continuous variation with little suggestion of discrete population structure (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on PCoA analysis of genomic data.

claim: The first PCoA axis correlates with latitude.
source: This analysis, which was based on genomic data with no geographic information included, showed that the samples largely formed a single cluster, with the first PCoA axis correlating with latitude (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on PCoA analysis and regression shown in Figure 1B inset.

claim: The first two PCoA axes explained 3.0% of the genomic variation among individuals.
source: Together, the first two PCoA axes explained 3.0% of the genomic variation among individuals.
evidence: Direct statement of PCoA results.

claim: Geographic distance between samples explained 2.3% of the variation in individual genomic distance.
source: The Mantel test, examining the correlation between geographic and genetic distance matrices, estimated that geographic distance between samples explained 2.3% of the variation in individual genomic distance, indicating weak, but statistically significant, isolation by distance (p=0.0001).
evidence: Based on Mantel test results.

claim: Isolation by distance in E. melliodora is weak but statistically significant.
source: The Mantel test, examining the correlation between geographic and genetic distance matrices, estimated that geographic distance between samples explained 2.3% of the variation in individual genomic distance, indicating weak, but statistically significant, isolation by distance (p=0.0001).
evidence: Based on Mantel test results with p=0.0001.

claim: Mean Fst between sampling sites is 0.04 with standard deviation of 0.02.
source: For all comparisons Fst was low (mean Fst = 0.04, sd = 0.02) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct statement of calculated Fst values.

claim: The maximum Fst of 0.10 occurs between sites 3 and 13, which are separated by over 1200 km.
source: The maximum Fst of 0.10 occurs between sites 3 and 13, which are separated by over 1200 km.
evidence: Direct statement of maximum Fst value and geographic distance.

claim: The first two axes of the PCoA of Fst between sampling sites explained 37.1% of variation.
source: In contrast, the first two axes of the PCoA of Fst between sampling sites explained a higher percentage of variation (37.1%).
evidence: Direct statement of PCoA results.

claim: All sites with more than four individuals genotyped had similar levels of allelic diversity and expected heterozygosity.
source: All sites with more than four individuals genotyped had similar levels of allelic diversity and expected heterozygosity (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on calculated diversity metrics.

claim: The GDM model with four environmental variables plus geographic distance explained 40% of the genetic differentiation (Fst) between sampling sites.
source: The GDM model with these four variables plus geographic distance explained 40% of the genetic differentiation (Fst) between sampling sites.
evidence: Direct statement of GDM model results.

claim: The four environmental variables in the final GDM model are isothermality, mean temperature of the coldest quarter, precipitation of the wettest quarter, and total soil nitrogen at 100–200 cm.
source: As a result, we included four environmental variables in the final model: isothermality (bioclimatic variable 3), mean temperature of the coldest quarter (bioclimatic variable 11), precipitation of the wettest quarter (bioclimatic variable 16), and total soil nitrogen at 100–200 cm (nitrogen at depth) (Figure 2).
evidence: Direct statement of model variables.

claim: The GDM model showed a positive non-linear relationship between environmental distance and genomic distance.
source: The GDM model showed a positive non-linear relationship between environmental distance and genomic distance (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on GDM analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cross validation of the GDM model showed satisfactory predictive power with mean correlation of 0.73.
source: To quantify the predictive power of the GDM model, we used a cross validation approach by generating 1000 models with a random 30% of sampling sites removed. GDM proved satisfactory at predicting genomic differences between removed sites (cross validation correlation mean = 0.73, standard deviation = 0.12).
evidence: Based on cross-validation analysis with 1000 iterations.

claim: The geographic spline predicted no genomic differentiation until close to 500 km.
source: The geographic spline predicted no genomic differentiation until close to 500 km, at which point an increase in geographic distance predicted an increase in genomic distance (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on GDM geographic spline shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Of the four environmental variables, nitrogen at depth showed the strongest relationship with genomic distance.
source: Of the four environmental variables, nitrogen at depth showed the strongest relationship with genomic distance, with changes in genomic distance predicted across the range of nitrogen values (Figure 2E).
evidence: Based on GDM splines shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: Mean temperature of the coldest quarter was the second strongest predictor of genomic distance.
source: Mean temperature of the coldest quarter was the second strongest predictor, showing changes in genomic distance predicted across the range of temperature values (Figure 2F).
evidence: Based on GDM splines shown in Figure 2E-H.

claim: The GDM model projected onto current environmental conditions partitioned the landscape into regions with different predicted genomic compositions.
source: The resulting map partitioned the landscape into a number of regions with different predicted genomic compositions, including northern coastal, northern inland, and southern regions (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on projection of GDM model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The middle north region and southern coastal areas show higher genomic vulnerability to climate change.
source: For the middle north region and the southern areas towards the coast (red in Figure 3B), the model predicted more intense natural selection in response to climate change, thus indicating that these areas should be prioritized for assisted migration.
evidence: Based on genomic vulnerability analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All fixed effects (sampling site, maternal line nested within sampling site, and experimental condition) were statistically significant for all three growth response variables.
source: The models for all three response variables showed that all fixed effects (sampling site, maternal line nested within sampling site, and experimental condition) were statistically significant at the p=0.05 level (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Based on linear mixed-effect model results.

claim: Experimental condition explained 1.2–8.1% of variation in growth traits.
source: Experimental condition explained a small percentage of the variation (1.2–8.1%), as did sampling site (1.8–17.7%).
evidence: Based on linear mixed-effect model results.

claim: Sampling site explained 1.8–17.7% of variation in growth traits.
source: Experimental condition explained a small percentage of the variation (1.2–8.1%), as did sampling site (1.8–17.7%).
evidence: Based on linear mixed-effect model results.

claim: Maternal line explained 10.6–27.6% of variation in growth traits.
source: Maternal line tended to explain a larger amount of variation (10.6–27.6%).
evidence: Based on linear mixed-effect model results.

claim: Most of the variation in growth traits remained unexplained (56.6–71.5%).
source: However, most of the variation remained unexplained (56.6–71.5%) (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Based on linear mixed-effect model results.

claim: None of the three growth response variables showed significant variation in phenotypic plasticity across sites.
source: None of the three response variables showed significant variation in phenotypic plasticity across sites (p>0.50 for all maternal line/sampling site by experimental condition interactions) (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Based on linear mixed-effect model interaction terms.

claim: Drought-treated seedlings had significantly lower stomatal conductance rates than well-watered ones.
source: The drought-treated seedlings had significantly lower stomatal conductance rates than the well-watered ones, indicating that the seedlings were affected by the watering treatment (p<0.00001) (Figure 6 and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of drought experiment data.

claim: Treatment explained 62.3% of variation in stomatal conductance.
source: Treatment explained most of the variation in stomatal conductance (62.3%), while maternal line and sampling site explained only a small amount of variation (5.8% and 0.9% respectively).
evidence: Based on linear mixed-effect model results.

claim: Seedlings subjected to drought conditions showed lower SLA values.
source: Consistent with this expectation, the seedlings subjected to drought conditions showed lower SLA values.
evidence: Based on measured SLA values in drought experiment.

claim: Seedlings from drier sampling sites showed higher SLA values than more mesic sites, contrary to expectation.
source: However, seedlings from drier sampling sites (D and T3) showed higher SLA values than more mesic sites (B, G, and 11), contrary to expectation (Figure 6).
evidence: Based on measured SLA values in drought experiment.

claim: None of the four drought experiment response variables showed significant variation in phenotypic plasticity across sites.
source: None of the four response variables showed significant variation in phenotypic plasticity across sites (p>0.13 for all maternal line/sampling site by experimental condition interactions) (Figure 6 and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Based on linear mixed-effect model interaction terms.

claim: Qst and Fst were not significantly different for measured traits, indicating that phenotypic differences between sites could be a result of genetic drift alone.
source: Qst and Fst were not significantly different, indicating that phenotypic differences between sites could be a result of genetic drift alone.
evidence: Based on Qst-Fst analysis comparing phenotypic and genomic differentiation.

claim: Seedling height showed non-significant differences between Qst and Fst suggesting local selection could be driving divergence.
source: While not statistically significant, seedling height did show differences between Qst and Fst in both hot (Qst-Fst = 0.33, p=0.11) and warm (Qst-Fst = 0.24, p=0.14) chambers. This indicates that local selection could be driving the divergence in height between sites, but our analysis lacked statistical power due to small sample sizes.
evidence: Based on Qst-Fst analysis with p-values indicating lack of statistical significance.

claim: Substantial variation in leaf shape was observed both among sites and within sites.
source: We noted substantial variation in leaf shape, both among sites and within sites (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on visual observation of leaf scans shown in Figure 7.

claim: The mean Fst of 0.04 in E. melliodora is consistent with microsatellite analysis of this species (Fst = 0.03).
source: We found little genomic divergence between sampling sites (mean Fst = 0.04), which is consistent with microsatellite analysis of this species (Fst = 0.03, (Broadhurst et al., 2018)) and population genetic analyses of other tree species (E. camaldulensis, Fst = 0.05, 0.08, (Butcher et al., 2009); E. globulus, Fst = 0.08, (Jones et al., 2002); Corymbia calophylla, Fst = 0.03, (Sampson et al., 2018); Pinus taeda, Fst = 0.04, (Eckert et al., 2010); Quercus robur, Fst = 0.07, (Vakkari et al., 2006); Quercus engelmannii, Fst = 0.04, (Ortego et al., 2012); Populus tremuloides, Fst = 0.03, (Wyman et al., 2003)).
evidence: Comparison with previous microsatellite study cited.

claim: The genomic divergence in E. melliodora is consistent with population genetic analyses of other tree species.
source: We found little genomic divergence between sampling sites (mean Fst = 0.04), which is consistent with microsatellite analysis of this species (Fst = 0.03, (Broadhurst et al., 2018)) and population genetic analyses of other tree species (E. camaldulensis, Fst = 0.05, 0.08, (Butcher et al., 2009); E. globulus, Fst = 0.08, (Jones et al., 2002); Corymbia calophylla, Fst = 0.03, (Sampson et al., 2018); Pinus taeda, Fst = 0.04, (Eckert et al., 2010); Quercus robur, Fst = 0.07, (Vakkari et al., 2006); Quercus engelmannii, Fst = 0.04, (Ortego et al., 2012); Populus tremuloides, Fst = 0.03, (Wyman et al., 2003)).
evidence: Comparison with multiple cited studies of other tree species.

claim: 'Local' in E. melliodora can be empirically defined as on the order of 500 km, which is substantially farther than current practice.
source: Examining the relationship between genomic and geographic distance, we are able to empirically define 'local' in this species to be on the order of 500 km, which is substantially farther than the current practice.
evidence: Based on GDM geographic spline showing no differentiation until 500 km.

claim: Restoration projects can and should source seed more broadly across the landscape for E. melliodora.
source: These results mean restoration projects can and should source seed more broadly across the landscape, with limited risk of mixing highly evolutionarily diverged material.
evidence: Inference based on finding of low genetic differentiation over 500 km.

claim: Incorporating more naturally occurring genomic variation can increase the adaptive potential of restored populations.
source: Incorporating more naturally occurring genomic variation can increase the adaptive potential of the restored populations by providing the substrate for adaptation to rapidly changing environmental conditions.
evidence: Logical inference from population genetics principles.

claim: The climate variables identified in the GDM model are predicted to change rapidly over time.
source: Of these variables, the climate variables are predicted to change rapidly over time.
evidence: Based on climate change predictions.

claim: Change in soil nitrogen content might occur over longer time scales than climate variables.
source: Change in soil nitrogen content might occur over longer time scales, but it is difficult to forecast due to complex biotic feedbacks (Brevik, 2013).
evidence: Inference supported by citation to Brevik, 2013.

claim: Key environmental variables may become uncoupled, resulting in less than ideal conditions for E. melliodora across the landscape.
source: The different time scales also highlight the important concern that key environmental variables may become uncoupled, resulting in less than ideal conditions for this species across the landscape.
evidence: Speculation based on different rates of environmental change.

claim: Previous niche modelling of E. melliodora found temperature and precipitation variables to be important, similar to the current analysis.
source: Previous niche modelling of E. melliodora examined environmental drivers of the distribution of the species (Broadhurst et al., 2018). Similar to our analysis, that analysis also found temperature and precipitation variables to be important, but the exact bioclimatic variables identified did not overlap.
evidence: Comparison with previous study cited.

claim: Niche modelling identifies drivers that define environmental tolerance of the species, while the current analysis identifies drivers for genomic variation within the species.
source: This is not unexpected given that niche modelling identifies drivers that define the environmental tolerance of the species, while the analysis presented here identifies drivers for genomic variation within the species.
evidence: Explanation of methodological differences.

claim: Many studies of within-species genetic variation in trees find temperature and precipitation variables to be the most important drivers.
source: Many studies of within-species genetic variation in trees find temperature and precipitation variables to be the most important drivers (Aitken et al., 2008); however, the exact variables vary and other variables are often found to play important roles.
evidence: General statement supported by citation.

claim: A quantitative genetics study of Eucalyptus delegatensis found that variables related to solar radiation contributed most to adaptive variability.
source: A quantitative genetics study of Eucalyptus delegatensis in Australia found that the variables that contributed most to the adaptive variability of the species were related to solar radiation (Garnier-Géré and Ades, 2001), which was not assessed in our study.
evidence: Comparison with cited study.

claim: The focus of this study was whole-genome population structure that reflects historical adaptation, gene flow, and demography.
source: The focus of this study was the whole-genome population structure that reflects historical adaptation, gene flow, and demography.
evidence: Direct statement of study focus.

claim: Analyses of individual genes was beyond the scope of this study due to low resolution GBS genotyping and limited extent of linkage disequilibrium in Eucalyptus.
source: Analyses of individual genes was beyond the scope of this study due to the low resolution GBS genotyping and the limited extent of linkage disequilibrium in Eucalyptus (Silva-Junior and Grattapaglia, 2015; Thumma et al., 2005).
evidence: Explanation of study limitations supported by citations.

claim: The results demonstrate a lack of strong population structure, indicating that using whole genome sequencing to identify adaptive alleles is feasible in E. melliodora.
source: However, our results demonstrate a lack of strong population structure, indicating that using whole genome sequencing to identify adaptive alleles is feasible in this species.
evidence: Inference based on population structure results.

claim: The Qst-Fst analysis indicates the possibility of local adaptation for seedling height.
source: For instance, the Qst-Fst analysis indicates the possibility of local adaptation for seedling height and a future study could identify the adaptive loci underlying plant height by targeting sampling sites segregating for this trait.
evidence: Based on Qst-Fst analysis results.

claim: The results of this study are promising for the future of E. melliodora across its native distribution.
source: The results of this study are promising for the future of E. melliodora across its native distribution.
evidence: Overall assessment based on study findings.

claim: High genomic and phenotypic diversity was found within sites and shared across the range of E. melliodora.
source: We found high genomic and phenotypic diversity within sites, as well as shared across the range.
evidence: Summary of genomic and phenotypic results.

claim: Naturally occurring variation in E. melliodora can provide a basis for adaptation to rapidly changing environments.
source: This naturally occurring variation can provide a basis for adaptation to rapidly changing environments and it should be incorporated into restoration projects through strategic seed sourcing.
evidence: Inference based on high levels of variation found.

claim: It remains to be determined whether human modifications of the landscape have disrupted historical patterns of gene flow in E. melliodora.
source: It is important to note that our genomic analyses were based on mature trees that predate extensive land clearing for agriculture. It remains to be determined whether human modifications of the landscape have disrupted the historical patterns of gene flow, resulting in more fragmented and inbred populations.
evidence: Speculation about potential impacts not assessed in the study.

claim: The landscape genomic model can guide seed selection by empirically defining local provenances and identifying variation suitable for predicted future climates.
source: Our landscape genomic model can guide seed selection by empirically defining local provenances and identifying variation suitable for predicted future climates.
evidence: Summary of model applications.

claim: Leaf samples were obtained from 39 sampling sites—38 sites across the species' native range and one site in Western Australia.
source: We obtained E. melliodora leaf samples from mature trees at 39 sampling sites—38 sites across the species' native range and a single site in Western Australia, well outside the species' natural distribution.
evidence: Direct description of sampling design.

claim: Samples were collected through a community science project.
source: We collected samples through a community science project described in Broadhurst et al., 2018 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct statement of collection method with citation.

claim: The study sequenced almost 260 million read pairs on an Illumina HiSeq2500.
source: We sequenced the library pool on an Illumina HiSeq2500 using a 101 bp paired-end protocol at the Biomolecular Resource Facility at the Australian National University, generating almost 260 million read pairs.
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing output.

claim: 11% of read pairs could not be assigned to a sample during demultiplexing.
source: We used AXE (v0.2.6, [Murray and Borevitz, 2017a)) to demultiplex the sequencing reads according to each sample's unique combinatorial barcode and were unable to assign 11% of read pairs to a sample.
evidence: Direct statement of demultiplexing results.

claim: 88% of reads successfully mapped to the E. grandis reference genome.
source: We aligned reads using bwa-mem (v0.7.5a-r405, [Li, 2013]), as paired reads (-p) and treating shorter split hits as secondary alignments (-M), with 88% of reads successfully mapped.
evidence: Direct statement of alignment results.

claim: The study used the E. grandis reference genome v2.0 for read alignment.
source: We aligned sequencing reads to the E. grandis reference genome (v2.0, [Bartholomé et al., 2015; JGI, 2015; Myburg et al., 2014]), including all nuclear, chloroplast, mitochondrial, and ribosomal scaffolds, but used only nuclear scaffolds for downstream analyses.
evidence: Direct statement of reference genome used.

claim: The study grew seedlings from six sites with six maternal lines per site.
source: We selected six sites (11, B, D, G, T1, T3; asterisks in Figure 1A) and six maternal lines per site that had sufficient seed.
evidence: Direct description of experimental design.

claim: For each maternal line, a minimum of 64 replicate seedlings were grown.
source: For each of the 36 maternal lines, we grew a minimum of 64 replicate seedlings, with four seeds planted per pot (6.5 cm x 6.5 cm x 20 cm pots with soil that was 80% Martin's mix and 20% sand).
evidence: Direct description of experimental design.

claim: Climate conditions in the growth chambers were determined with SolarCalc to mimic average summer conditions and hotter conditions (5°C temperature increase).
source: Climate conditions were determined with SolarCalc (Spokas and Forcella, 2006) to mimic average summer conditions (sampling site 11) and hotter conditions (5°C temperature increase; sampling site T3).
evidence: Direct description of experimental conditions.

claim: The experimental treatment ran for 12–14 weeks with phenotypic measurements at five time points.
source: We ran the experimental conditions for 12–14 weeks and took phenotypic measurements at five time points:1, 2, 3, 5, and 11 weeks after the experimental treatment began.
evidence: Direct description of experimental timeline.

claim: The outdoor drought experiment was conducted on 16 week old seedlings after completion of the chamber experiment.
source: After completion of the chamber experiment, we conducted an outdoor covered drought experiment on the 16 week old seedlings.
evidence: Direct description of experimental timeline.

claim: 160 seedlings from five sampling sites with four maternal lines per site were selected for the drought experiment.
source: We selected 160 seedlings from five sampling sites, with four maternal lines per site.
evidence: Direct description of experimental design.

claim: GBS sequencing reads are available at the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject PRJNA413429.
source: GBS sequencing reads are available at the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra) under BioProject PRJNA413429.
evidence: Direct statement of data availability.

claim: Growth experiment data and analysis scripts are available at https://github.com/LaMariposa/emelliodora.
source: Growth experiment data and scripts for genomic and phenotypic analyses are available at https://github.com/LaMariposa/emelliodora (Supple, 2018; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/emelliodora).
evidence: Direct statement of data availability.
